Acrylic paint-along · beginner

A black-capped chickadee on a curved autumn branch

Start on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

17 stepsCanvas: 14 x 11 inFocal point: the bird's head and eye Light: a low, warm sun at the upper right, behind and to the right of the birdHow this lesson was made

What you need

Tubes

  • Titanium white
  • Lemon yellow
  • Flesh tint
  • Permanent red
  • Ultramarine
  • Dark green
  • Burnt sienna
  • Burnt umber
  • Raw umber

Brushes

  • 1 inch flat: Blend the gold glow into the misty skyFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • #8 round: Paint the sunRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • 1/2 inch flat: Pull down the far misty trunksFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • old stiff brush: Dab the hazy orange foliageOld stiff flat: worn, splayed bristles, for rough texture like grass and foliage
  • 3/4 inch flat: Paint the branch in bark brownFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • #10 round: Paint the four leaves warm goldRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • #10 filbert: Block in the body warm goldFilbert: flat with a rounded end, for soft-edged shapes
  • #6 filbert: Paint the wing and tail blue-grayFilbert: flat with a rounded end, for soft-edged shapes
  • 1/4 inch angle: Stroke in the dark wing feathersAngle: flat cut on a slant, for crisp corners and curves
  • #6 round: Paint the black cap and bibRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • #8 filbert: Shade the lower bellyFilbert: flat with a rounded end, for soft-edged shapes
  • liner: Paint the legs and toes darkLiner: long, very thin bristles, for fine lines like twigs and grass
  • small round: Add the gray light on the toesRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press

Also

  • A 14 x 11 in canvas, landscape (hang it that way), and masking tape to mark halves and quarters along its edges.
  • Water jar and paper towel
  • Palette or paper plate for mixing

Your paints

Every paint in the lesson. You don't have to mix them all at the start: each step lists the paints it uses with their recipes, so you can mix a little as you go before it dries. Parts are by volume.

Before you start

Mark halves and quarters on tape

Run a strip of masking tape along the top edge of the canvas and one down a side, and mark the middle and the quarters on each. On your 14 x 11 in canvas the marks across the top are 3 1/2 in apart and the marks down the side 2 3/4 in apart. Every step's Where picture has the same lines, so you can find its place on your canvas. (Chalk lines on the canvas would be painted over by the first coat; the tape stays.)

The transfer outline (optional)

The outlines of the main shapes, on the same quarter grid as your tape: 1 The four leaves; 2 The chickadee. Before the stage that starts one, you can lightly chalk its outline on the canvas, using the tape marks to place it.

Strokes to try on scrap paper first

Each one's card is open in the step that first uses it.

  • X stroke, first in step 1.
  • Small circles, first in step 2.
  • Pull-down, first in step 3.
  • Dabbing, first in step 4.
  • Thick to thin, first in step 5.
  • Dry brush, first in step 6. Try it on scrap paper first: wipe the brush until it leaves broken marks.
  • Press and lift, first in step 7. Try a row of them on scrap paper first.
  • Building from pieces, first in step 9.
  • Curved strokes, first in step 10.
  • Liner work, first in step 16. Try a few lines on scrap paper first.

The basics

Before you start not checked yet

Before you start

Not checked yet

  • Two water jars: one to rinse the brush, one kept clean for thinning paint. A big clear jar shows when the rinse water is dirty.
  • A rag or paper towel, to wipe the brush between colors.
  • Put out bigger puddles of paint than you think you need. Big puddles stay wet longer than small smears.
  • Lay your colors out the same way every time, so they're easy to find and don't get dragged into each other.
Keep your colors clean not checked yet

Keep your colors clean

Not checked yet

  • Wipe the brush on a rag between colors.
  • Rinse it fully before going into white.
  • Rinse often. Dirty water tints every color with the last one.
  • Mix on the palette, not on the canvas. Two or three colors at most: stop when the color is right.
Colors dry darker not checked yet

Colors dry darker

Not checked yet

  • Acrylic looks lighter when wet than when dry.
  • Before a big area, paint a test swatch and let it dry before judging the mix.
Fixing a mistake not checked yet

Fixing a mistake

Not checked yet

  • Acrylic is forgiving. Let the area dry, then paint over it and try again.
  • Don't keep working a spot that's half dry. Leave it, work somewhere else, and come back.
Keep paint from drying on the palette not checked yet

Keep paint from drying on the palette

Not checked yet

  • Acrylic on a brushstroke stays wet for only a few minutes.
  • Mist the palette lightly with a spray bottle now and then. Only lightly: too much water weakens the paint.
  • Cover the paint when you aren't using it.
Let each layer dry not checked yet

Let each layer dry

Not checked yet

  • Between steps, the paint underneath should be dry to the touch. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  • Painting into half-dry paint drags it up and turns it gooey and muddy.
  • Thick paint can feel dry on top and still be wet inside. Give thick areas longer.
  • Fine lines and light colors over dark especially need a dry layer underneath.
Light colors over dark need more than one coat not checked yet

Light colors over dark need more than one coat

Not checked yet

  • One coat of white or a light color over a dark one usually looks gray and patchy.
  • Expect two or three thin coats, letting each dry. Use the paint thick, with little water.
Making a color lighter or darker not checked yet

Making a color lighter or darker

Not checked yet

  • To lighten: add the color to the white a little at a time, not white to the color.
  • White also dulls a color. Too much turns it chalky.
  • To darken: add the dark into the lighter mix in small amounts.
  • For the next lighter value of something, start from the mix you already have and add white, so the colors stay related.
One light direction not checked yet

One light direction

Not checked yet

  • Pick where the light comes from and put every highlight on that side.
  • Each thing is built the same way: the whole shape in a darker or middle value, a lighter value on the side facing the light, then the lightest on a small area at the very edge. Each covers less than the one before.
The ugly stage not checked yet

The ugly stage

Not checked yet

  • Partway through, every painting looks flat or wrong. That's normal. Keep building.
  • Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.
  • Details come last, and only on shapes that are already right.
How much water not checked yet

How much water

Not checked yet

  • Keep water to about half the mix or less. More than that makes weak, see-through color that can lift when you paint over it.
  • For covering, use the paint thick, with little or no water.
  • After rinsing, wipe the metal part of the brush dry.

The misty sky 2 steps

STEP 1 OF 17 · The misty sky, 1 of 2

Blend the gold glow into the misty sky

  1. Inside the outlined area: the whole canvas.
  2. Paints, top to bottom: Warm gold, then Misty blue-gray.
  3. Mix enough Warm gold for this step and steps 7 and 9; cover it between them.
  4. Mix enough Misty blue-gray for this step and step 10; cover it between them.
  5. Brush: 1 inch flat. Load: One or two colors on the brush. How much of each is on it controls the blend.
  6. Short strokes that cross each other in two directions, like overlapping X shapes.
  7. It should leave a soft, slightly textured blended fill with visible criss-cross marks.

Tip: The light comes from a low sun at the upper right, so every highlight in this painting goes on the right and top sides. Start with the gold around where the sun will be, then work the blue-gray in from the left and bottom edges, crossing strokes where they meet. Paint straight through where the bird, branch and leaves will go. The X strokes leave soft patches: let a few darker blue-gray vertical smudges stay at the far left and low in the middle, as hints of far trees.

STEP 2 OF 17 · The misty sky, 2 of 2

Paint the sun

  1. Let the misty sky and glow dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Rinse the brush fully first: this is the lightest paint yet.
  3. Inside the outlined area. Its top is about 1 in from the top edge, and its right side is about 4 in from the right edge; it's about 1 in wide and 1 in tall.
  4. Paint: Sun cream.
  5. Brush: #8 round.
  6. Small circles with the tip of the brush, working from the middle of the sun outward.
  7. It should leave a bumpy, soft edge.
  8. Watch out: The edge is too hard. Fix: soften it with lighter passes. On a cloud, smudging with a finger works too.
  9. Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.

Tip: The sun is a circle about 1 inch across, a little right of the canvas center and about 1 1/2 inches down from the top, as the Where picture shows. Keep its edge soft so it melts into the glow.

The far woods 2 steps

STEP 3 OF 17 · The far woods, 1 of 2

Pull down the far misty trunks

  1. Let the misty sky dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Rinse the brush well first. Dirty water tints every color with the last one.
  3. Inside the outlined area, top to bottom to the right edge. Its left side is about 2 1/2 in from the right edge.
  4. Paint: Trunk blue-gray.
  5. Brush: 1/2 inch flat. Load: Load the brush, then wipe it until only a little paint is left.
  6. Stroke straight down from the top of each trunk to the bottom of the canvas.
  7. It should leave soft, streaky, see-through trunks with the mist showing a little through them.

Tip: There are two trunks, side by side, running the full height of the canvas near the right edge, with a thinner one fading in just left of them. Keep them pale and soft: they are far away in the mist, so no texture.

STEP 4 OF 17 · The far woods, 2 of 2

Dab the hazy orange foliage

  1. Let the far misty trunks and the misty sky dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area. It reaches all four edges of the canvas.
  3. Paint: Hazy orange.
  4. Brush: old stiff brush. Load: Little paint, fairly dry.
  5. Tap with the tip of the brush. The more you tap one spot, the more solid it gets.
  6. It should leave dots or dappled patches that get more solid the more you tap.
  7. Watch out: Blobs instead of dots. The brush is too wet or holds too much paint. Fix: wipe most of the paint off on a paper towel and tap again.
  8. Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.

Tip: Most of the patches sit on the right half, around and over the trunks, with a few lower left and along the bottom. Keep them loose and soft-edged, with blue-gray mist showing between them; they are far away.

Motion. Tap with the tip of the brush. The more you tap one spot, the more solid it gets.

Then. Tap a lighter mix on the lit side, leaving the darker taps showing underneath.

If it goes wrong.

  • Blobs instead of dots. The brush is too wet or holds too much paint. Wipe most of the paint off on a paper towel and tap again.
  • A patch went too solid. Tap over it with a lighter or darker mix to break it up.

The branch 2 steps

STEP 5 OF 17 · The branch, 1 of 2

Paint the branch in bark brown

  1. Let the far woods and the misty sky dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area. It reaches all four edges of the canvas.
  3. Paint: Bark brown.
  4. Brush: 3/4 inch flat.
  5. Press the full width of the brush for the thick part, then turn onto its edge or tip and lighten the pressure. With an angle brush, the lighter you press, the thinner the line.
  6. It should leave a branch that starts wide at the trunk and tapers to thin twigs at the right.

Tip: The trunk rises up the left edge and bends into the big branch, which arches across the canvas under the bird and thins out toward the lower right. Pull each stroke along the branch, wide at the trunk end and thin toward the twigs at the right. The two thin stems that hang down to the lower leaves are part of this step: carry them right on into where the leaves will go, as their center lines.

STEP 6 OF 17 · The branch, 2 of 2

Dry-brush the light along the branch

  1. Let the branch and the far woods dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area. It reaches all four edges of the canvas.
  3. Paint: Bark tan.
  4. Brush: 1/2 inch flat. Load: A dry brush, no water. Load only the tip, then wipe most of the paint off on a paper towel. It should feel dry and hard to apply.
  5. Light pressure, skimming the surface.
  6. It should leave feathery, broken, see-through marks that catch the canvas texture. Never a solid area.
  7. Leave what step 5 painted showing around these marks, as in the Result picture.
  8. Watch out: It went on solid. The brush was too loaded. Fix: let it dry, then dry-brush the base color back over part of it.
  9. Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.

Tip: The light is from the upper right, so the tan goes on the top edge of the branch and the right side of the trunk. Leave the brown showing along the underside.

The four leaves 2 steps

STEP 7 OF 17 · The four leaves, 1 of 2

Paint the four leaves warm gold

  1. Let the branch and the far woods dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Optional: lightly chalk its outline first, from the transfer outline in Before you start, placed with the tape marks.
  3. Inside the outlined area, top to bottom. Its left side is about 1 in from the left edge and its right side is about 2 1/2 in from the right edge.
  4. Paint: Warm gold.
  5. Brush: #10 round. Load: Paint loaded well into the belly of the brush, creamy, not runny.
  6. Touch down with the tip, press so the belly spreads, then pull and lift so the stroke ends on the tip.
  7. It should leave a leaf shape, wide where you pressed and pointed where you lifted, with jagged edges.
  8. Watch out: A blob instead of a teardrop. Too much paint, or too slow a lift. Fix: use less paint and lift faster.

Tip: Two leaves hang at the top left, near the trunk, and two hang below the branch on the right. Each leaf is a pointed, jagged shape a little longer than it is wide; press the brush in the middle of the leaf and lift toward its tip.

The chickadee 7 steps

STEP 9 OF 17 · The chickadee, 1 of 7

Block in the body warm gold

  1. Let the far woods and the misty sky dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.

Paint the white cheek

STEP 16 OF 17 · Legs and feet, 1 of 2

Paint the legs and toes dark

  1. Let the chickadee and the branch dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Rinse the brush well first. Dirty water tints every color with the last one.
  3. Inside the outlined area. Its bottom is about 4 in from the bottom edge, and its left side is about 5 1/2 in from the left edge; it's about 2 1/2 in wide and 1 1/4 in tall.
  4. Paint: Chickadee black.
  5. Brush: liner. Load: Thin the paint with water until it flows like ink: swirl the brush in water, then in the paint. Reload often.
  6. Hold the brush upright, with light, steady pressure. Pull each leg down from the body, then each toe as a short curve over the branch.
  7. It should leave thin, flowing lines.
  8. Watch out: Skippy, broken lines. The paint is too thick. Fix: add water.

Tip: The two legs come down from the bottom of the body, about 1 inch apart, and the toes wrap over the top of the branch. Paint the legs as short lines and the toes as small curved hooks.

How Claude read your photosubject, light, layers

Before starting

Subject: A black-capped chickadee perched on a curved brown branch, four autumn leaves, a misty blue-gray forest with orange foliage and a soft sun glow upper right

Found in the image: just the picture (an AI-made painterly image, no bars, borders, text or watermark)

Done: none

Why: Everything in the image is part of the scene.

Fitted to your canvas

Canvas: 14 x 11 in, landscape (11x14)

Done: crop

Left out: about 15%: a strip at the left edge (part of the trunk's left side and orange dabs) and a strip at the right edge (misty trunks and foliage).

Why: fit-canvas picked a free crop: the 3:2 photo trimmed at left and right to the 14:11 canvas, keeping the bird and its branch whole.

Beginner version

What made it too busy: No tiny separate things; the background foliage is already loose dabs; no detail inside big shapes beyond the bird's feathers (the subject); parts fit within 8.

Why: Every 0c answer is no, so the lesson is made from the canvas-fitted photo.

A chickadee on an autumn branch, lit from behind by a low sun at the upper right. What matters: the bird's black cap and bib against the warm glow, the soft misty background, and the curve of the branch. The hard part for a beginner is keeping the background soft and far away while the bird and leaves stay crisp, and placing the bird's head, wing and bib right.

Subject: A black-capped chickadee on a curved autumn branch
Focal point: the bird's head and eye
Light: a low, warm sun at the upper right, behind and to the right of the bird

What it saw, back to front

  1. Misty sky and glow
  2. The branch
  3. The four leaves
  4. The chickadee
  5. Legs and feet
Why this techniquePaint along, back to front
ChosenPaint along, back to frontStart on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

Owner's pick for acrylic beginners (docs/decisions.md 2026-10-19): white canvas, back to front, each step one brush move. The picture is a soft painterly background with a bird, branch and leaves in front: exactly the back-to-front paint-along order.

Passed onBlock in, then build up (acrylic-block-in-beginner)

The owner follows paint-along tutorials; v2 step and stage ranges and max_mixes are set on the paint-along technique.

How the paint recipes were worked out14 paints, free

Paint doesn't mix like light on a screen: blue and yellow make green, not gray. So the recipes come from a pigment mixing model (Mixbox), not a guess. For each paint it tried every simple recipe from your tubes, up to three colors plus white, and kept the one that lands closest to the color in the painting. Delta E is how far off it lands: under 2 is hard to see, under 5 is close, and over 8 means these tubes can't quite make it.

    Mixer: 3 parts flesh tint, 1 part ultramarine, a touch of dark green, a touch of white

  • Hazy orange Delta E 0.8
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

  • Bark brown Delta E 1.5

Why the steps go in this order17 steps

Back to front: the misty sky and glow over the whole canvas, the sun, the far trunks, the far foliage, then the branch (behind the bird), the leaves, the bird from its body to its marks, and the feet last because they grip over the branch.

  1. 1. Blend the gold glow into the misty sky

    The whole canvas first: the glow and mist are behind everything, painted straight through.

  2. 2. Paint the sun

    The brightest spot sits on the dry sky before anything in front of it.

  3. 3. Pull down the far misty trunks

    The far trunks are the next layer back to front, over the dry sky.

  4. 4. Dab the hazy orange foliage

    The far orange foliage sits over and around the trunks, still in the far distance.

  5. 5. Paint the branch in bark brown

    The branch is behind the bird and leaves, so its dark base comes first.

  6. 6. Dry-brush the light along the branch

    The lit top of the branch goes on its dry dark base, before anything sits on it.

  7. 7. Paint the four leaves warm gold

    The leaves hang from the branch's stems; their gold base comes after the branch.

  8. 8. Add the red-orange to the leaves

    The red-orange goes over the dry gold base.

  9. 9. Block in the body warm gold

    The bird's whole shape goes down first, as the base for its marks.

  10. 10. Paint the wing and tail blue-gray

    The wing and tail are the biggest marks on the body.

  11. 11. Stroke in the dark wing feathers

    The dark feathers go over the dry blue-gray wing.

  12. 12. Paint the black cap and bib

    The cap and bib, the darkest marks and the focal point, after the body and wing.

  13. 13. Paint the white cheek

    The white cheek fills between cap and bib, light over the gold, after the black is dry.

  14. 14. Shade the lower belly

    The shadow side of the belly, darker before the cream (darkest first).

  15. 15. Light the breast cream

    The lit breast last on the body, toward the sun.

  16. 16. Paint the legs and toes dark

    The legs and toes cross over the branch and body, so they come after both.

  17. 17. Add the gray light on the toes

    The light on the toes is the last small highlight.

Where Claude drew diagrams3 steps, free

Three steps block in shaped things a beginner couldn't start from the picture alone: the branch (a trunk that bends into an arch and forks), the leaves (pointed, lobed shapes), and the bird (body, head, tail). The rest are fills, repeated marks, or passes over a shape already there.

  • Step 5: Paint the branch in bark brown beginner check

    Noticed: The trunk and branch appear whole, with twigs forking off; where the arch starts and joins isn't obvious.

    Pieces: Trunk first as one tall tapering band, then the arch from its base thinning to the right, then the twigs.

  • Step 7: Paint the four leaves warm gold beginner check

    Noticed: Four pointed, lobed leaf shapes appear whole in one step.

    Pieces: A long teardrop for the middle, a pointed lobe on each side, then the stem.

  • Step 9: Block in the body warm gold beginner check

    Noticed: The whole bird appears as one shape; proportions of head, body and tail matter.

    Pieces: Body oval first, head circle on its upper right overlapping it, tail wedge down to the lower left.

What the reviewer caught8 notes

A second Claude, with fresh eyes and none of this reasoning, compared each picture with its neighbors and the finish. It gets two rounds of fixes, then stops; anything still off is flagged on its step. A third checked each step's words against a measured map of what the picture changed, asking whether a beginner following them would get there.

  • Finish check First finish: the background blue-gray turned a brighter, saturated sky blue and lost its haze; fixed in the one redo.
  • Text check: missing Step 1: faint far-trunk smudges at the left and bottom in the sky picture had no line (fixed)
  • Text check: missing Step 5: the stems that become the lower leaves' center lines are painted in the branch step without a word (fixed)
  • Text check: flat Step 8: the gold leaves also get orange edges; text only covered the red leaves (fixed)
  • Text check: drift Step 9: a small hole under the bib is a rough background fill until the cap and chest steps, and a sliver of the upper-left red leaf changes in the bird's steps (left: the outline model takes the red leaf or drops the cap when given points there)
  • Text check: missing Step 12: the eye's white glint shows with no line (fixed)
  • Text check: too_much Step 15: a darker tan shadow on the lower belly appeared in the cream step (split)
  • Text check: missing Step 15: the beak's top lightens in this step (fixed)
